runs.text:
Every generation needs three files to get going: a style guide, a corpus passage, and a prompt template. The runner reads the frontmatter of each one, hashes the whole file, and saves that hash next to the output.

Here's how the pieces fit together. The guide's body becomes the system prompt. The passage gets dropped into the template to form the user prompt — and that prompt goes to the child process over standard input, not as an argument. Why? So you never have to worry about shell quoting or command-line length limits messing things up.

From there, the runner spawns the Claude Code CLI with an explicit argument vector and asks for a JSON envelope back. It waits, and if things drag on, it escalates: a polite termination signal first, then a forced kill if needed.

The runner parses whatever comes back, even when the process exits non-zero — because that's exactly what a refusal looks like: a failing exit code paired with a well-formed envelope that spells out the reason.

Either way, success or failure, every field in that envelope gets written to disk. Same goes for the argument vector, the resolved model, the token counts, and how long the whole thing took.

argv:
Rewrite the text following the Microsoft writing style.

Sound like a helpful colleague chatting with the reader, not a manual. Use
contractions everywhere they'd naturally occur, address the reader directly as
"you", and reach for everyday words over formal ones. A sentence fragment is
fine when it lands the point — don't force every thought into a full clause.

Open with the single thing the reader most needs to know, then explain. Keep
sentences short and let the page's shape (headings, short paragraphs) do some
of the work.

Use sentence case for any heading. Use the active voice and the present tense.
Tell the reader exactly what to do and what happens next, in a tone that feels
like a quick conversation rather than a document.

Skip jargon, hedging, and anything that talks down to the reader — but don't
skip the personality. A little warmth and a casual aside are welcome.

Here's what kicks off a generation: three files — a style guide, a corpus passage, and a prompt template.

The runner reads the frontmatter of each one, hashes the whole file, and saves that hash next to the output. Simple as that.

## How the prompt comes together

The guide's body becomes the system prompt. The passage gets dropped into the template to form the user prompt. That user prompt goes to the child process over standard input, not as a command-line argument — so you never have to worry about shell quoting rules or hitting a length limit. One less thing to break.

## Running the CLI

The runner spawns the Claude Code CLI with an explicit argument vector and asks for a JSON envelope back. Then it waits, with a timeout that starts polite (a gentle termination signal) and escalates to a forced kill if needed.

Here's the important part: the runner parses the response even if the process exits non-zero. Why? Because that's exactly how a refusal shows up — a failing exit code paired with a well-formed envelope that explains why.

## What gets saved

Every field from that envelope lands on disk, whether things succeeded or not. Alongside it, you get:

- The argument vector
- The resolved model
- Token counts
- Wall-clock duration

Nothing gets thrown away, even on failure. Especially on failure, really — that's often when you need the details most.
